name: Harder Kulm
label: Harder Kulm
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Viewing platform above the town with views over Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.

text.description: Harder Kulm is the viewpoint above Interlaken, at 1,322 metres on the western end of the forested Harder ridge. It photographs well because you look straight down on the towns of Interlaken and Unterseen and the flat land between them, known as the Bödeli. Your eye then follows the Lütschine valley southwards to the high peaks of the Bernese Alps. That gives you a foreground, a middle distance and a mountain backdrop in one frame. The top is occupied by a castle-like restaurant and an observation platform next to it, which makes a natural place to take pictures. The Harderbahn funicular climbs from Interlaken in about eight minutes. Its upper station is some five minutes' walk from the restaurant, so allow a little time for that last stretch. For phone photos, keep the horizon level and use the town below for scale. A wide shot shows the whole valley. A zoomed shot isolates the peaks at the far end. Take a few frames at different zoom levels rather than relying on one. If the sky is hazy or cloudy, concentrate on the town and the valley floor and leave the summits as a bonus.
text.geographic_location: Harder Kulm sits on the western end of the Harder ridge, directly above the towns of Interlaken and Unterseen. It belongs to the municipality of Unterseen, in the Bernese Oberland.
text.directions_text: From Interlaken, take the Harderbahn funicular up to the Harder Kulm station; the ride takes about eight minutes. From the upper station it is some five minutes on foot to the restaurant and observation platform. Check the official site before you go for running times. The phone icon on the map is about 320 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view of the town and valley. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to include the platform or railing in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Bernese Alps at the end of the valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 320 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Use the observation platform beside the restaurant and face south, looking over Interlaken and up the Lütschine valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the town and valley fill most of the frame. Keep the phone level so the valley does not look tilted. Take one wide frame, then a zoomed frame of the high peaks. Use the town roofs below as foreground for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the distant mountains to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its detail. For a sweeping view, try panorama mode and pan slowly from left to right.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, as cloud can hide the peaks. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, but check the funicular's running times on the official site first.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is reached by a tourist funicular and the top has a restaurant, so check the official site before you go for running times and any ticket rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The view from the platform faces broadly south, towards the Bernese Alps.
Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Cloud or haze can hide the high peaks.
The platform may be busier in fine weather around midday.
The funicular may be ticketed and have set running times, so visitors should check the official site.
The observation platform next to the restaurant makes a natural place to take pictures.

name: Interlaken Ost railway station
label: Interlaken Ost
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Interlaken Ost' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3114762827: the OpenStreetMap point 'Interlaken Ost'.
notes: Gateway station for trains to Jungfraujoch and Lauterbrunnen.

text.description:
Interlaken Ost is the eastern of the town's two railway stations. It was once called Interlaken Zollhaus and took its present name in 1890, when the Bernese Oberland railway arrived and made it much busier. Today three lines meet here: the BLS Thunersee line, the Zentralbahn Brünig line and the Bernese Oberland railway towards Lauterbrunnen and Grindelwald. Every passenger service ends here, and trains of several operators and two gauges (standard and metre) use the station, which gives you plenty of railway scenes to photograph. Ships on Lake Brienz also use a quay at the station, reached along the Aare, so water and rail sit close together.

The station photographs best as a simple 'arrival in Interlaken' picture. Stand at the phone icon on the map, at the front of the station. A Commons photo shows the station with the Aare canal in frame, so try to include the canal alongside the building, but confirm the exact standing point on site. That gives you the building and the water in one frame. Keep your phone level so the building lines stay straight, and wait for a few people to walk through to give a sense of scale. If you want a second angle, the ferry terminal next to the station is another place people photograph from. Stay behind the platform lines if you go onto the platforms, and keep out of the way of passengers.
text.geographic_location: Interlaken Ost is at the eastern end of Interlaken, in the Swiss canton of Bern, where the rail lines to Lake Brienz, Lake Thun and the Lauterbrunnen and Grindelwald valleys meet. The Aare canal runs alongside the station.
text.directions_text: If you arrive by train from Bern, Basel, Lucerne, Lauterbrunnen or Grindelwald, you are already at Interlaken Ost, so just walk out to the front of the station. Interlaken West is the town's other station, so check that you are at Ost rather than West. The phone icon on the map is at the station itself, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the station front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the building and canal in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a train nose or the station name.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. A Commons photo shows the station with the Aare canal in frame, so look for a spot where the canal is in view alongside the building, and confirm the exact standing point on site.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the station building up with one of the horizontal lines so it does not lean. If the canal is in view, place it along the lower or side edge so the water leads the eye towards the building. Keep your arms steady and take a few frames as people pass. As an alternative angle, try the ferry terminal next to the station.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky does not wash out. Use Live Photos if you want to catch a train pulling in or the movement of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight, in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the front of the station is usually less harsh. Early in the day it is often quieter.

text.access_note: This is a working railway station, so check the official site before you go for any rules about photographing on the platforms.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is generally softer than midday light.
Early in the day the station front is often quieter.
The ferry terminal is next to the station and is another place people photograph from.
The exact standing point with the Aare canal in frame is based on a Commons photo and should be confirmed on site.

name: Harderbahn
label: Harder Funicular
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zwei-Seen-Steg' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Zwei-Seen-Steg' (way/194072044): middle (18 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/35398117: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Harderbahn' (239 m long).

text.description:
The Harderbahn is the funicular that climbs the Harder, the ridge on the north side of Interlaken. It opened on 15 May 1908 and is 1,435 metres long. The ride takes ten minutes. The track was laid in a gentle curve rather than a straight line, so that it would not scar the hillside. The lower station is at 550 metres, and the top station is a short walk from the Harder Kulm viewpoint at 1,321 metres. There is a pagoda-style restaurant up there too.

For photographs, the best result is the view from the top. From here you look over Interlaken, which sits between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, with the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau behind. This view does not include the railway itself. If you want the funicular in your picture, the lower station is the place for it. The steep track and the cars leaving the station, with the station building in the frame, make a good second shot.

The walkway is the popular spot, so expect company. Quieter shots can be taken from the sides. Funicular tickets and running times can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Harderbahn's lower station is on the north side of the River Aare, close to Interlaken Ost train station, and the line climbs the Harder above the town.
text.directions_text: The lower station is about a five-minute walk from Interlaken Ost train station. Ride the Harderbahn up (about ten minutes). The Zwei-Seen-Steg is at the summit, by the upper station end. The Harder Kulm viewpoint and the restaurant are about a five-minute walk from the top station. The walking time from the station to the walkway itself is not confirmed. Check the official site for the season and timetable before you set out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the town-and-lakes view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the lakes in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull in the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Zwei-Seen-Steg (upper station end, Harder Kulm summit). Interlaken between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, with the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau behind; it does not frame the railway itself. At the summit by the upper station end. From here your phone looks over Interlaken between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, with the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau behind. The railway itself is not in this view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the town and the two lakes in the lower half of the frame and the peaks above. If the walkway is crowded, step to its sides for a quieter angle. For a shot of the funicular itself, the lower station is a good alternative. Its steep track and the cars leaving the station, with the station building in the frame, are what you want.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the town or the mountains to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky keeps its colour. Wipe your lens before shooting, as it is often smudged by then.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, according to several guides. Check the last descent time at the station so you are not caught out.

text.access_note: The summit is reached by the Harderbahn, which is a ticketed funicular with a summer timetable, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tapping on the screen to focus and lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright skies from washing out.
Phone lenses are often smudged, so wiping the lens before shooting helps.
The last descent time varies and should be checked at the station.

name: Unterseen
label: Unterseen Old Town
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Untere Gasse' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Untere Gasse nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1682700: large area 'Unterseen' (8785 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic old town on the Aare with wooden houses and the covered bridge.

text.description:
Unterseen is the old riverside town on the north bank of the Aare, just across the water from Interlaken. It photographs well because its historic core is compact and full of character, and the best frame is along Untere Gasse, the old main lane. Wooden houses line both sides, so a view from one end fills the picture with a row of facades. A travel guide describes this street as set-like and a good choice for townscape shots away from the tourist bustle.

The town has a long story. King Rudolf I von Habsburg gave permission for a stronghold between the two lakes in 1279, and Unterseen was founded on 13 July of that year. It burnt down in 1470, and Bern oversaw the rebuilding with the town house at the centre. The town wall and moat were taken down in the early 19th century. Today it is a small place of about 5,760 people, and on a clear day the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau can be seen from the town.

For a phone, the lane is the main subject. Stand at either end, keep the phone level, and let the line of houses lead the eye along the street. If you have time, walk down to the river afterwards: the Bühlmattbrücke gives a view across the Aare toward the timber houses, with mountains behind. Spielmatte, by the old mill, is another riverside option.
text.geographic_location: Unterseen is the historic town on the north bank of the Aare, directly across the river from Interlaken, on the flat Bödeli land between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz. The old town's main lane is Untere Gasse.
text.directions_text: From Interlaken, cross the Aare to the north bank, where the old town of Unterseen begins. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the street looks natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit more of the facades into a narrow lane. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as woodwork, shutters and window boxes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Untere Gasse. The old town's main lane lined with wooden houses, framed from one end so the row of facades fills the picture. Untere Gasse is a street you can walk along. From there you can see the row of wooden houses along the old town's main street, and the facades fill the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical edges of the houses up with them, so the buildings do not lean. Keep the street running down the middle and let the rooflines lead into the distance. For a second view, try the Bühlmattbrücke over the Aare, looking toward the timber houses with the river in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facades to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the wood colours stay rich. Use ultra-wide only when you need it, as it can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually suits the street best, with softer light and fewer people. In the evening the riverside views are worth a second look.

text.access_note: Untere Gasse is a public street in the old town; if you also visit the riverside, bridges or any buildings, check the official site before you go.

name: Höhematte
label: Höhematte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Höheweg' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Höheweg nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM R1173420 (Höhematte): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Central park meadow with the classic view of the Jungfrau.

text.description: The Höhematte is the broad green lawn in the middle of Interlaken, a Grand Tour of Switzerland photo spot with a view of the Jungfrau. Stand on the Höheweg promenade and the open grass fills the foreground, with the snow-capped Jungfrau massif rising behind it. The lawn has been protected since 1864 and is a free public park. The view works well on a phone because the flat grass gives you a clean foreground and the mountains sit above it. The Höheweg runs past the town's grand hotels, and they can frame the picture at the edge of the shot. The Grand Tour of Switzerland marks the spot near the Armin-Schärz-Brunnen as the official photo spot. Paragliders sometimes land on the lawn, which can add a bright splash of colour to the frame. It can also mean the foreground is busy or briefly blocked, so wait a moment and try again. If you want the mountains more directly ahead, walk out onto the Höhematte itself, where Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau line up over the open grass. Take a shot from each place and compare. Whether the peaks show at all depends on the weather, so check the sky before you plan your visit.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Interlaken, the Höhematte is the large lawn beside the Höheweg promenade, which is lined with grand hotels. The photo spot is at Höheweg 57a, opposite the Casino.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Interlaken and head for the Höheweg promenade. The lawn lies just beyond it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lawn with the Jungfrau behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the hotels along the promenade in the frame as well. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the peaks closer, and to pick out a paraglider coming in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Höheweg (photo spot near the Armin-Schärz-Brunnen, facing the Höhematte lawn). The open green lawn of the Höhematte with the snow-capped Jungfrau massif rising behind it. The open grass fills the foreground and the snow-capped Jungfrau massif rises behind it. For Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau straight ahead, walk onto the Höhematte itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, so the mountains get most of the picture and the grass becomes a calm band beneath. Use the hotels or trees at the edge of the frame as a border. If you walk out onto the lawn, try a second shot with the three peaks directly ahead. If a paraglider lands, Live Photos can catch the movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountains to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the snow keeps its detail instead of turning white. Phone panorama mode can work for the full sweep of lawn and peaks, but hold the phone steady and keep still people out of the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, because the Jungfrau is easy to lose in cloud. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the peaks.

text.access_note: The Höhematte is a free public park, but paid parking runs along the Höheweg and near the park, so check the official site before you go if you are driving.

name: Heimwehfluhbahn
label: Heimwehfluh
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Heimwehfluh' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Heimwehfluh' (node/6109341037): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/651536138: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line '' (45 m long).

text.description:
The Heimwehfluhbahn is a short, steep funicular that climbs the Heimwehfluh hill above Interlaken. It was built between 1904 and 1906 and is only 197 metres long, but it rises 102 metres, with a maximum gradient of 69%. Its two wooden cars date from 1906, and the curtained, unglazed windows give it a deliberately old-fashioned look. A single ride takes about 2 minutes. At the top, 680 metres above sea level, there is a restaurant, an observation tower, a model railway and a children's playground.

The railway photographs well because the setting does the work. From near the restaurant terrace at the summit you look across the Interlaken plain to both lakes, with the slope of the railway in the frame. That gives a wide picture in which the railway sits in its landscape. If you want the vintage character, the red-and-cream cars at the valley station, with the hillside rising behind the line, make a good second picture. The observation tower gives a higher and wider panorama of Interlaken, Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, with the funicular far below.

Take a few frames at each level rather than one. Keep the track and the lakes both in view so the shot reads as a railway with a view. Look for the line of the rails to lead the eye down the slope. The funicular is the usual way up, so check the official site before you go for running times and fares.
text.geographic_location: The Heimwehfluhbahn climbs the Heimwehfluh hill on the edge of Interlaken, in the Swiss Canton of Bern. The summit looks over the Interlaken plain and both lakes.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check the official site for the location of the funicular's valley station before you set out. Take the funicular up to the summit. The suggested viewpoint is near the restaurant terrace area, so check on site that you are in the right place. The line of the railway lies about 157 m to the north-east of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole plain, lakes and railway together. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the slope and the line of the railway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Heimwehfluh (restaurant terrace at the summit station). The Interlaken plain and both lakes seen from the summit, with the upper station and its slope in the frame. The terrace is the suggested viewpoint, so check on site. From here the Interlaken plain and both lakes spread out in front of you, with the slope in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line so the lakes and plain fill the picture. Let the slope and the line of the rails sit to one side as a point of interest. Hold the phone level, because the wide lens bends the horizon quickly. For a different picture, go to the valley station for the red-and-cream cars with the hillside behind, or up the observation tower for a higher, wider panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lakes to set focus and exposure, then pull the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright. If you are shooting through the terrace railings or glass, keep the lens close to a gap and avoid reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the lakes and mountains are easiest to see. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.

text.access_note: The terrace is at the top of a funicular, so check the official site before you go for running times, seasons and fares.

name: Unspunnen Castle
label: Unspunnen Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Burgruine Unspunnen' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/969543801: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Burgruine Unspunnen' (51 m across).
notes: Castle ruin on a wooded hill south of town.

text.description:
Unspunnen Castle is a ruin on a rocky spur above the valley. A round tower and stretches of old wall are still standing. It was probably built in the early 12th century, and the name Uspunnun first appears in records in 1232. After 1762 the castle was left to fall into disrepair. It became famous through the Unspunnenfest of 1805, which led to regular cleaning and repairs. The festival of traditional Swiss competitions is still held in the fields below.

It photographs well because you can stand among the old stonework and still see the Jungfrau massif and the valley towards Interlaken behind it. That puts the castle and the mountains in one frame, which is hard to find elsewhere nearby. The courtyard and the rampart walls on the open side facing the Jungfrau give the best view. Use the tower and walls as a dark, textured foreground, and let the peaks fill the background.

The ground is uneven, so wear sturdy shoes and watch your footing while you compose a shot. If the mountains are hidden by cloud, the ruin still makes a good close-up of stone, walls and sky. For a second view, the Burgweg footpath below shows the ruin on its spur with the valley opening out behind.
text.geographic_location: Unspunnen Castle stands on a rocky spur in the municipality of Wilderswil, overlooking Interlaken. The Unspunnenfest fields lie below the ruin.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed near the ruin. It lies in the municipality of Wilderswil, above Interlaken. The phone icon on the map is at the ruin itself, so once you are inside the walls you are already in place. Allow time for the last stretch on uneven ground. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and walls with the mountains behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the stonework and want the whole courtyard or rampart in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the Jungfrau massif closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the round tower and surviving walls are in the foreground, with the Jungfrau massif and the valley towards Interlaken behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower or a section of wall on one third, leaving the mountains and valley on the other two thirds. Keep the horizon level. Use an edge of wall or an opening as a natural frame. As an alternative, the Burgweg footpath below shows the ruin on its rocky spur with the valley and mountains opening out behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mountains to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its detail and the stone stays dark but readable. Try a Live Photo if there is wind or cloud moving across the peaks. Panorama mode works along the rampart if you move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day so the Jungfrau massif is visible. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework than midday.

text.access_note: The ruin is free and open all year, but the ground is uneven and sturdy shoes are advised; photography is not restricted.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light on stonework.
Cloud can hide the Jungfrau massif, so a clear day gives the best view.

name: Interlaken Monastery
label: Interlaken Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Schloss Interlaken' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Schloss Interlaken' (node/2123811689): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1775392: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Former Augustinian monastery with its church and castle courtyard.

text.description:
Interlaken Monastery was a house of Augustinian canons from about 1133 until 1528, when it was closed during the Reformation. It is now a Swiss heritage site of national significance. Today the old monastery buildings and the later castle share one set of grounds, and the castle has remained the administrative centre of the Interlaken district. That is why the place looks like a mix of church, cloister and stately house rather than a single building.

It photographs well because the church steeple and the 14th-century tower, the most striking part of the site, rise above the lawns with mountains behind. From there the monastery buildings are just to the south, so you can step back, turn and fit the whole group into one frame.

A second, quieter view is from the Schlosspark. The tree-lined grounds show the Gothic cloister gallery and the church tower across the lawns. In 1746-50 the west wing was pulled down and the newer castle built in its place, so look for the different building styles side by side. Keep to the exterior and the cloister, as parts of the complex are government offices.
text.geographic_location: In Interlaken, in the castle grounds (Schloss Interlaken) beside the castle church and the Schlosspark. The old monastery buildings share the site with the later castle.
text.directions_text: From Interlaken, head for Schloss Interlaken and the castle church. Once you are in front of the Schlosskirche, the monastery buildings are a very short way to the south, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole group of buildings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the steeple and tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the castle church (Schlosskirche)). The monastery-castle complex with its church steeple, the 14th-century tower that is the most striking part of the site, framed by the mountains behind. At Schloss Interlaken, in front of the castle church (Schlosskirche). From here the monastery-castle complex lies just to the south, with the church steeple and the 14th-century tower set against the mountains behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the steeple on one of the vertical lines, with the mountains behind it. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. For a quieter alternative, walk into the Schlosspark and shoot across the lawns to catch the cloister gallery and church tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the pale walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework does not wash out. Use the 0.5x lens only if you need it, as it can stretch the edges of the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework, and early in the day the grounds are often quieter.

text.access_note: The grounds are open to the public, but parts of the complex house government offices and the interior is restricted, so photograph the exterior and cloister and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework.
The grounds are often quieter early in the day.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch the edges of buildings.
